5  Local examples

https://www.geoboundaries.org/

I am assuming you want more mapping after the first exercise so lets explore some local examples that you can get started with!

5.1 Preparation

Load packages

Load packages is using the p_load command

pacman::p_load(
  rio,           # to import data
  tidyverse,     # to clean, handle, and plot the data (includes ggplot2 package)
  OpenStreetMap, # to add OSM basemap in ggplot map
  sf,            # to manage spatial data using a Simple Feature format
  readr,          # read in csv file
  tmap          # to produce simple maps, works for both interactive and static maps
  )

The downloaded binary packages are in
    /var/folders/3v/_s9tgz1d7h9b4nqhbkx95gc40000gs/T//RtmpFGqpqO/downloaded_packages

5.2 Using OpenStreetMap

OpenStreetMap is a collaborative project to create a free editable map of the world. The underlying geolocation data (e.g. locations of cities, roads, natural features, airports, schools, hospitals, roads etc) are considered the primary output of the project.

First we load the OpenStreetMap package, from which we will get our basemap.

Then, we create the object map, which we define using the function openmap() from OpenStreetMap package (documentation). We provide the following:

  • upperLeft and lowerRight Two coordinate pairs specifying the limits of the basemap tile
    • In this case you will see we have put in the max and min from the mosquito occurrence dataset we will be using, so the map will respond dynamically to the data
  • zoom = (if null it is determined automatically)
  • type = which type of basemap - we have listed several possibilities here and the code is currently using the first one ([1]) “osm”
  • mergeTiles = we chose TRUE so the basetiles are all merged into one
Note

Mosquito occurrence I searched for and downloaded mosquito occurrence data from the iNaturalist site - searching for any Culicidae occurrences in Sarawak. You can load it in as the csv file is saved in the data/mapping/iNat-mosquito-obs directory

mosqutio <- read_csv("data/mapping/iNat-mosquito-obs/observations-545115.csv")
Rows: 58 Columns: 51
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (31): uuid, observed_on_string, time_observed_at, time_zone, user_login...
dbl  (10): id, user_id, num_identification_agreements, num_identification_di...
lgl   (9): sound_url, captive_cultivated, private_place_guess, private_latit...
date  (1): observed_on

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

This data is loaded directly as it appears from iNaturalist, we can take a look at what it contains first

Now we can use the coordinates in the columns labeled latitude and longitude to set the boundaries for our basemap.

# Fit basemap by range of lat/long coordinates. Choose tile type
map <- OpenStreetMap::openmap(
  upperLeft = c(
    max(mosqutio$latitude, na.rm = T),
    max(mosqutio$longitude, na.rm = T)
  ),
  # limits of basemap tile
  lowerRight = c(
    min(mosqutio$latitude, na.rm = T),
    min(mosqutio$longitude, na.rm = T)
  ),
  zoom = NULL,
  type = c(
    "osm",
    "stamen-toner",
    "stamen-terrain",
    "stamen-watercolor",
    "esri",
    "esri-topo"
  )[1]
)

If we plot this basemap right now, using autoplot.OpenStreetMap() from OpenStreetMap package, you see that the units on the axes are not latitude/longitude coordinates. It is using a different coordinate system. To correctly display the case residences (which are stored in lat/long), this must be changed.

# Plot map. Must use "autoplot" in order to work with ggplot
autoplot.OpenStreetMap(map)

Thus, we want to convert the map to latitude/longitude with the openproj() function from OpenStreetMap package. We provide the basemap map and also provide the Coordinate Reference System (CRS) we want. We do this by providing the “proj.4” character string for the WGS 1984 projection, but you can provide the CRS in other ways as well. (see this page to better understand what a proj.4 string is)

# Projection WGS84
map_latlon <- openproj(map, projection = "+proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84 +datum=WGS84 +no_defs")

Now when we create the plot we see that along the axes are latitude and longitude coordinate. The coordinate system has been converted. Now our cases will plot correctly if overlaid!

# Plot map. Must use "autoplot" in order to work with ggplot
autoplot.OpenStreetMap(map_latlon)

See the tutorials here and here for more info.

When we have a basemap with lat/long coordinates, we can plot our cases on top using the lat/long coordinates of their residence.

Building on the function autoplot.OpenStreetMap() to create the basemap, ggplot2 functions will easily add on top, as shown with geom_point(). Now we can start plotting those mosquito occurrence records

# Plot map. Must be autoplotted to work with ggplot
autoplot.OpenStreetMap(map_latlon) +                 # begin with the basemap
  geom_point(                                       # add xy points from linelist lon and lat columns 
    data = mosqutio,                                
    aes(x = longitude, y = latitude),
    size = 1, 
    alpha = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE) +                          # drop legend entirely
  labs(x = "Longitude",                             # titles & labels
       y = "Latitude",
       title = "Mosquito Occurence Data Sarawak")

Contoured density heatmaps

For this data set there are not too many occurrences, but in some instances it may be useful to visualize it as a Contoured density heatmaps. Remember in our mosquito metadata each row with an observed occurrence.

To create a Contoured density heatmap

  1. Create basemap tile from OpenStreetMap, as described above
  2. Plot the cases from mosqutio using the latitude and longitude columns
  3. Convert the points to a density heatmap with stat_density_2d() from ggplot2,

When we have a basemap with lat/long coordinates, we can plot our cases on top using the lat/long coordinates of their residence.

Building on the function autoplot.OpenStreetMap() to create the basemap, ggplot2 functions will easily add on top, as shown with geom_point() below:

# begin with the basemap
autoplot.OpenStreetMap(map_latlon)+
  
  # add the density plot
  ggplot2::stat_density_2d(
        data = mosqutio,
        aes(
          x = longitude,
          y = latitude,
          fill = ..level..,
          alpha = ..level..),
        bins = 10,
        geom = "polygon",
        contour_var = "count",
        show.legend = F) +                          
  
  # specify color scale
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "black", high = "red")+
  
  # labels 
  labs(x = "Longitude",
       y = "Latitude",
       title = "Distribution of Mosquito occurrences")

5.3 Using the sf package

To use this package you will need a shape file.

A google search for “Malaysia Shapefile” lead me to this resource which contains shape file for the states in Malaysia.

my = read_sf("data/mapping/my_shp/my.shp")

The package tmap offers simple mapping capabilities for both static (“plot” mode) and interactive (“view” mode) with just a few lines of code. The tmap syntax is similar to that of ggplot2, such that commands are added to each other with +. Read more detail in this vignette.

tmap_mode("plot")
ℹ tmap mode set to "plot".
tm_shape(my) +               # admin boundaries shapefile
  tm_polygons(col = "#F7F7F7")+    # show polygons in light grey
  tm_borders(col = "#000000",      # show borders with color and line weight
             lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("name")

Including an interactive view using tmap_mode("view")

tmap_mode("view")
ℹ tmap mode set to "view".
tm_shape(my) +               # admin boundaries shapefile
  tm_polygons(col = "#F7F7F7")+    # show polygons in light grey
  tm_borders(col = "#000000",      # show borders with color and line weight
             lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("name")

We can also plot using ggplot2 package

ggplot(data=my) + 
  geom_sf(aes(fill=name))

Adding in our records to our tmap

Covert the mosquito dataframe to a sf with function st_as_sf() to create the new object we call mosqutio_sf. This designated the columns longitude and latitude as coordinate columns, and a coordinate reference system (CRS) has been assigned for when the points are displayed.

# Create sf object
mosqutio_sf <- mosqutio %>%
     sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)

Now we overlay our occurrence data over the interactive tmap

tmap_mode("view")
ℹ tmap mode set to "view".
tm_shape(my[6,]) +               # admin boundaries shapefile
  tm_polygons(col = "#F7F7F7")+    # show polygons in light grey
  tm_borders(col = "#000000",      # show borders with color and line weight
             lwd = 2) +
  tm_text("name") +
tm_shape(mosqutio_sf) +
  tm_dots(size=0.08, col='purple', alpha = 1) +
  tm_layout(title = "Mosquito Occurence Data Sarawak") 

── tmap v3 code detected ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
[v3->v4] `tm_dots()`: use 'fill' for the fill color of polygons/symbols
(instead of 'col'), and 'col' for the outlines (instead of 'border.col').[v3->v4] `tm_dots()`: use `fill_alpha` instead of `alpha`.[v3->v4] `tm_layout()`: use `tm_title()` instead of `tm_layout(title = )`

5.4 Another options with additional boundaries

Lets redo a similar map to the one above but this time we have sourced data from a different repository.

We want to include information at the district level - this might be handy if you later want to be able to be plots about prevalence at that level.

To do this we need a map with this information - lucky the Department of Statistics Malaysia hosts this on their GitHub.

This time we can call the file directly from the repository (it achieves the same outcome as above but we don’t have to rely on a static data file in our local repository!)

tmp_geojson <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dosm-malaysia/data-open/master/datasets/geodata/administrative_2_district.geojson",
  tmp_geojson
)
my_district <- read_sf(tmp_geojson)

We can use tmap to make a simple country map

sf_use_s2(FALSE)
Spherical geometry (s2) switched off
tmap_mode("plot")
ℹ tmap mode set to "plot".
tm_shape(my_district) +               # admin boundaries shapefile
  tm_polygons(col = "#F7F7F7")+    # show polygons in light grey
  tm_borders(col = "#000000",      # show borders with color and line weight
             lwd = 2)

And again with the interactive view using tmap_mode("view")

tmap_mode("view")
ℹ tmap mode set to "view".
tm_shape(my_district) +               # admin boundaries shapefile
  tm_polygons(col = "#F7F7F7")+    # show polygons in light grey
  tm_borders(col = "#000000",      # show borders with color and line weight
             lwd = 2)

Using ggplot2 we can easily code each district by state.

ggplot(data=my_district) + 
  geom_sf(aes(fill=state))
